title: AR Software

sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOCs course on Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
We are in lecture number 11 where we are discussing AR software.
We will continue our discussion on AR software.
So, earlier we talked about the basic categories of AR software.
We learned about different ways to categorize and different ways to view AR software.
One such category is based on the skill requirement from the part of the developer.
Another categorization can be based on the platform, the hardware, the operating system, or a combination of both, or even mobile versus desktop platforms.
Mobile versus wearable platforms.
So, different ways to categorize.
Then we have also seen that it is possible to categorize based on technology used, particularly on tracking.
We are following the skill requirement-based categorization in this discussion.
So, we have covered low-level libraries and frameworks, which is one of the categories.
Then we started our discussion on the second category, which is rapid prototyping tools.
We partly covered that; we are going to continue our discussion on that category, and also we are going to cover the other categories in this particular way of looking at AR software.
So, let us continue our discussion with rapid prototyping tools.
So, earlier we talked about flash-based tools.
Let us see non-flash-based tools, if there are any.
So, we mentioned that it is possible to avoid, I mean it is possible to have non-flash-based tools.
Now, it is also possible to avoid third-party browser plugins altogether.
So, earlier tools that we talked about were primarily meant for browser-based experiences.
where we require plugins, say for example flash-based plugins or non-flash system-based plugins.
But when we are talking about other tools, we can say that it is also possible to avoid third-party browser plugins altogether.
Instead, you can build your own using HTML, WebGL, or other such web component technologies.
You can write your own program.
If you have mastery over such technologies, then you don't need to use any third-party plugin.
Instead, you can go for writing your own code to create a fast prototype.
There are also non-web-based authoring tools meant for mobile and desktop platforms.
So both environments are supported with such tools.
For example, Open Frameworks.
As the name suggests, this is a framework which is a combination of multiple libraries.
It is meant for desktop and mobile platforms.
Now, Open Frameworks is quite widely used.
It is an open-source C++ middleware library.
With Open Frameworks, it is easy to build interactive experiences while building an AR application.
As the name suggests, and we have already mentioned, it provides a framework for combining a wide range of different interactive technologies.
So, the framework provides support for tracking, rendering, as well as interaction.
All three are supported.
For example, An AR application could be developed by combining a tracking library such as AR Toolkit with hand tracking, a 3D scene graph for rendering, and audio playback libraries.
So, we can combine more than two libraries for generating different effects in our proposed application.
For mobile applications, one useful prototyping tool is Wikitude.
Typically, such tools are AR browser applications.
Wikitude is one such example.
Now, these are free applications.
They run on mobile devices.
The computation does not take place on the mobile device.
Instead, they connect back to some servers for providing content and specifying user interface elements on mobile.
So, mobile is primarily treated as a client device or as a rendering device only; actual computation may take place on a backend server, not on the mobile.
So if the developers have their own content, then it will be easier or faster to prototype the ideas.
If the content is not there, the developer has to depend on some default content provided by such tools, which may reduce some sort of flexibility, but still it can be used.
That is about the second category.
Now, let us move our attention to the third category, that is, plugins to existing tools.
Partly we have talked about this in the previous category as well.
Here the idea is that when we are talking about software libraries, they require programming skills to use them.
You have to first understand and then use them.
So, one has to learn or master the libraries.

As opposed to that, now suppose that one is already aware of some interactive 2D or 3D content authoring tool, some tool that the user is already aware of, which may not be relevant at this stage for AR or VR system development or prototype development, but it is relevant for 2D or 3D content authoring.
So, in that case, the user does not need to understand or master a new tool completely from scratch.
What the user or developer can do is use plugins to existing such software.
These plugins add AR-specific functionalities to the tools.
So, the tools the user may be aware of which may not support AR, Content development or your system development whereas plugins if added to the known tool can provide that support.
So, the developer does not need to learn everything from scratch instead the developer can rely on the knowledge of that original tool and the developer needs to understand the plugin only.
The requirement of understanding the system thus reduces.
So, plugins are therefore useful when one already knows how to use the authoring tool with which the plugin is being added.
If the user does not know the authoring tool, then of course it makes no sense; the user has to learn everything from scratch.

As we have already mentioned, plugins simply add, some AR visualization and tracking functions to the existing authoring tool and it relies on functions provided by the main authoring tool for content authoring.

So, if you know the original tool then you can create your own content and then use the AR plugin for adding some functionalities related to tracking related to visualization of or 3D registration of digital content over real world view.
Some example plugins, let us see.

There are actually many interactive 3D graphics authoring tools to create interactive 3D applications such as Unity, Vizard, Lumion, Now, most of these tools have their own plugins for AR visualization.
So, they come with AR-based plugins.
The Unity tool has the widest range of solutions available for AR visualization.
For example, AR Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works can be one such plugin.
It can provide both marker and image-based or computer vision-based tracking and AR visualization support.
Similarly, the Vuforia tracking library has an AR plugin that works with Unity 3D.
So, Vuforia can be used as a plugin with Unity 3D to create AR applications, particularly mobile AR applications for both iOS and Android platforms.
So what are the pros?
We have already discussed when we are using a plugin-based approach, plugin-based tools.
So they provide an easy and quick method for developing AR applications.
But there are cons, there is, I mean, a negative side also.
User interface and interaction design can be limited to those provided by the authoring tool.
So the underlying authoring tool provides such support whereas plugins provide AR support.
Now the support provided by the underlying authoring tool restricts the developer's flexibility in deciding on different interaction methods or interface look and feel.
Software and hardware configuration also depends on what is provided by the tool.
So again, flexibility is lost.
Content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software.
So if you have some multimedia content, then to play that content, you have to, in most cases, not always, in most cases, you may have to depend on proprietary players.
And that again reduces some sort of flexibility.
Now, these are cons.
So, there is a positive side, there is a negative side.
And you know, as we all know, any approach will have both sides.

In this case, if we wish to resolve those issues, those cons or the negative sides, what we can do is we can rely on the hard way, that is we can use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries and build our own system from scratch rather than depending on some third-party tool.
That is applicable for any higher-level tool as such.
Now, let us move to the last category, that is standalone authoring tools.
So, here the idea is that standalone applications are there that allow users to create their own AR experiences with no programming experience.
So, even if someone does not have any programming experience, he or she can still be able to build an AR application using such authoring tools.
Unlike plugins, these tools do not require any additional software to work.
So, plugins require A basic software, a basic authoring tool to work on which AR support will be provided through a plugin.
In this case, they are standalone; they come as a complete package with content authoring as well as AR support.
So, they do not require or depend on any other tool.
And these authoring tools provide different sets of functions, as is obvious.
So, they support scene construction and animation, and also support adding interactive behavior.
So, these are typically common function sets that are supported by such standalone authoring tools.
Some of these tools only provide scene construction functions, while others have the full capability of building complex interactive behavior.
So, they come with different strengths.

come in different strengths; some provide limited support, some provide extensive support, which is again quite common in different software packages Now, most of these tools come with some sort of graphical user interface for the developer to create an application, create an experience.
Now, these GUIs are drag-and-drop type.
So, they allow drag-and-drop type interaction with the GUI to create an experience.
In that sense, they do not require—the developers do not require any coding as such.
But for flexibility, some sort of coding support, if the developer knows it, can be provided using scripting languages.
Users with basic PC skills could easily learn and use them, as coding is not required.
So, useful for non-programmers who want to build AR applications without actually going through learning coding skills.

However, as I said, absolute zero coding based applications will be limited in their utility as compared to some sort of advanced systems with scripting support, with scripts that will be providing more flexibility.
An example of such standalone authoring tools is the Wikitude Studio.
It is a web-based authoring tool.
It allowed users to create rich mobile AR content and also deploy either onto the Wikitude AR browser app or even create a custom mobile app.
So, users can either develop a system and deploy it on a browser app or can build and deploy it as a mobile app.
The studio is a package that comes with all these supports.
Now, this studio is no longer supported since last year.
But they are still in use.
The studio supported various types of media including 3D models and animations which can be registered to the real world.
So that is one example of the full standalone content authoring tool or AR application authoring tool.
which requires no coding skills.
There are many other such applications.
So with that, we can conclude our discussion on AR software.
So in summary, what we can say is that we have learned the basic idea of AR software.
We have tried to understand the different tools and packages that are available in terms of four categories.

The categories are based on programming skill required, At one extreme, we have the highest programming skill required when we are dealing with low-level libraries and frameworks, whereas on the other hand, at the other extreme, we require the least programming skill when we are dealing with standalone authoring tools.
In between, there are other categories such as rapid prototyping tools and one more category on plugins to existing systems.
We have also gone through the basic idea of each of these categories with some examples to understand them to some extent.

Next, in our next lecture, we will cover another important topic that is very much relevant to be able to fully understand, build, and deploy any, Extended reality systems, be it virtual reality or augmented reality, that is where human factors affect our experience in these domains.

So, we will discuss that by first discussing the idea of interactive systems, the role of human factors in interactive system building and deployment, and the factors that are most relevant for AR and VR experiences.
So, I hope you have enjoyed the content, understood the topics covered, and learned about AR software.
The topics that I have covered here are mostly taken from this reference.
You are advised to go through this reference if you can access it.
So with that, I would like to conclude this lecture.
See you in the next lecture.
Thank you, goodbye, and happy learning.

parts.objective: Contrast methods for developing AR prototypes, including using frameworks and custom code

key_points.text: AR software development can use custom web components (HTML, WebGL) to avoid third-party browser plugins.
Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library for building interactive desktop and mobile AR experiences.
Wikitude is a mobile AR browser application where computation often occurs on a backend server, not the mobile device.
AR software can be categorized based on skill requirements from the developer, platform, or technology used.

terms.name: WebGL
terms.definition: WebGL is a web component technology that allows developers to build their own programs for fast prototypes without needing to use third-party browser plugins.

terms.name: Open Frameworks
terms.definition: Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library that acts as a combination of multiple libraries. It allows users to build interactive AR experiences and provides support for tracking, rendering, and interaction.

terms.name: AR Toolkit
terms.definition: AR Toolkit is cited as an example of a tracking library that can be combined with other libraries, such as a 3D scene graph, to develop an AR application.

terms.name: Wikitude
terms.definition: Wikitude is an example of a useful prototyping tool for mobile applications; it is an AR browser application that runs on mobile devices.

terms.name: Backend server
terms.definition: Backend server is the external system to which mobile devices connect to receive content and specify user interface elements, handling the actual computation of the AR application.

terms.name: Client device
terms.definition: Client device is the mobile unit in the context of mobile AR that is primarily treated as a rendering device, even though the actual computation may be handled by a backend server.

terms.name: Rendering device
terms.definition: Rendering device is a mobile unit that is used for displaying content in an AR application, while the actual computation for the application may take place on a separate backend server.

parts.objective: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using plugins to existing authoring tools for AR development

key_points.text: Plugins extend existing content authoring tools by adding AR-specific functionalities, allowing developers to rely on prior tool knowledge instead of learning from scratch. (57, 58, 60)
The benefits of using plugins include offering an easy and quick method for developing AR applications. (76)
Disadvantages of plugins include limited user interface flexibility and dependency on proprietary player software. (78, 80, 83, 84)
To resolve the limitations of plugin-based approaches, developers can choose to use low-level software development tools and build systems from scratch. (89, 90)

terms.name: Plugin
terms.definition: A plugin is an add-on functionality that can be introduced to an existing software tool to provide AR-specific features, such as visualization and tracking, while relying on the main tool for content creation.

terms.name: Software library
terms.definition: A software library is a set of underlying code that requires the developer to first understand and master the programming skills to utilize it, allowing for the building of a system from scratch.

terms.name: Content authoring tool
terms.definition: A content authoring tool is an existing interactive 2D or 3D software used to create content; it may not inherently support AR or VR, but it serves as the host for plugins.

terms.name: AR visualization
terms.definition: AR visualization is the function that allows for the display of digital content, such as 3D registration, over a view of the real world.

terms.name: Tracking
terms.definition: Tracking is the process that allows digital content to be correctly registered over the real world view, which can be done using various methods like marker-based, image-based, or computer vision-based methods.

terms.name: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tool
terms.definition: An interactive 3D graphics authoring tool is a program, such as Unity, that is used to create interactive 3D applications and which often includes or supports its own specific AR-based plugins.

parts.objective: Distinguish standalone authoring tools from plugins and describe how they function

key_points.text: Standalone authoring tools allow users to create AR experiences without needing programming experience (92, 93).
Standalone tools are complete packages that include content authoring and AR support, unlike plugins (94, 95, 96, 97).
These tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior (99, 100).
Most standalone authoring tools use drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces, though scripting can add flexibility (103, 104, 106, 107).

terms.name: Standalone authoring tool
terms.definition: Standalone authoring tools are complete packages that allow users to create their own AR experiences without requiring prior programming experience or depending on additional software.

terms.name: Plugin
terms.definition: Plugins are components that provide AR support within a basic software package, requiring that foundational software to function.

terms.name: Wikitude Studio
terms.definition: Wikitude Studio is a web-based authoring tool used to create rich mobile AR content, capable of deploying the experience onto a dedicated browser app or a custom mobile application.

terms.name: Mobile augmented reality content
terms.definition: Mobile AR content is rich media created by authoring tools that can be used to build an AR experience and deployed onto mobile devices.

parts.objective: Summarize the basic ideas, tools, and categories of AR software

key_points.text: AR software tools and packages are categorized based on the programming skill required.
AR software categories range from low-level libraries (highest skill) to standalone authoring tools (least skill).

objectives.text: you'll be able to contrast methods for developing AR prototypes, including using frameworks and custom code
you'll be able to compare the advantages and disadvantages of using plugins and distinguish between standalone authoring tools and plugins
you'll be able to summarize the basic ideas, tools, and categories of AR software

lecture_goal: analyze the various development methods, tool integrations, and categories that define AR software.
